newsitem.title: USA: Italy can cut deficit to 3 pct of GDP - IMF official.
newsitem.headline: Italy can cut deficit to 3 pct of GDP - IMF official.

text.p: Italy's goal of lowering its state deficit to 3 pct of GDP in 1997 is realistic, and its announced budget measures are credible, an International Monetary Fund official said.

In addition, the lira's value against other currencies is in an acceptable zone and the prospect of Italy entering the European Monetary Union should open the door to an interest rate drop, Massimo Russo, head of the IMF European Department, said.
"The goal of reducing the deficit to 3 pct of GDP is rather realistic, since it is based on a growth forecast lower than the one set by the IMF," Russo said at a press conference.

"We believe in the measures announced in the 1997 budget bill" Russo said. But he said the IMF would be able to give a full judgement only when all the specific measures called for by the budget bill, aimed at cutting the deficit by 62.5 billion lire overall, have been defined.
Russo said he sees nothing wrong with the Italian proposal for a one-time 12 trillion lire levy dubbed the "tax for Europe".
"It is legitimate and useful", Russo said, but cautioned that it will not exempt Italy from future structural measures, which "remain necessary".

The prospect of entering the EMU, "is positive for a drop in interest rates," Russo said. Russo added that given the current 450-basis-point differential between Italian and German short-term interest rates "Italian interest rates could drop even if German rates should rise."
Should costs for industry (through labour flexibility) also come under control, Italy would start "threading a virtuous path," he said.

The lira's wxchange rate "is currently in an acceptable zone. At 1,200 to the deutsche mark it was not aligned. Now it lies within an equilibrium zone" Russo said, adding that "we do not want to see the lira devalued further".

The credibility of Italy's intent in pursuing the Euro rests also in the fact that "when a government sets the goal of entering the UME as a political target, it will do all that is necessary to achieve it," Russo said.

Russo avoided the issue of whether other measures may be necessary for Italy to meet the Maastricht criteria, but said that "if growth in Europe will be lower than forecast, there will be problems for everyone".
He said he did not believe Itlay's neighbors were plotting to keep it out of the EMU.
"We can't see evidence of plots against Italy. The major European countries are most interested in seeing Italy in the Euro, to avoid the risk of (lira) devaluations," Russo said.

Recent statments by Spanish and French officials questioning whether Italy would qualify for, later retracted, "may have something to do" with oncoming negotiations on the level at which the lira will reenter the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, Russo admits.
As to the Euro, Italy must however ensure it will be able to maintain its convergence and stability criteria after entering, "otherwise it would be better for it to wait".
The IMF "welcomes the further effort Italy is making" and had actually suggested it a year ago, Russo points out..
Italy "starts out from a more difficult situation. The acceleration towards the EMU is a recent decision. It is a good decision".
